title: Cache Invalidation
subtitle: Solving one of computer science's hardest problems: CDC-driven invalidation, race-free leases, and multi-region cache coherence.
keyTakeaways: Relying on dual-writes in application code (`db.update()` then `redis.del()`) fails when the process crashes between the two calls or when multiple services mutate the same DB table.
Change Data Capture (CDC) tailing the database WAL/binlog (via Debezium + Kafka) decouples cache invalidation from application code and guarantees eventual convergence.
Memcached Leases (or Redis version tokens) solve the classic Stale-Set race condition between a concurrent cache-miss reader and an invalidating writer.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Cache Invalidation is a foundational architectural concept in distributed systems. Solving one of computer science's hardest problems: CDC-driven invalidation, race-free leases, and multi-region cache coherence. Fundamentally, Consider what happens when Reader A gets a cache miss, reads `v1` from the DB, and pauses due to a GC pause or network blip. Meanwhile, Writer B updates the DB to `v2` and runs `DEL key` on the cache. Finally, Reader A wakes up and executes `SET key v1`—poisoning the cache with stale data until the TTL expires! Meta solved this in Memcached (`McLease`) using 64-bit Lease Tokens.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Relying on dual-writes in application code (`db.update()` then `redis.del()`) fails when the process crashes between the two calls or when multiple services mutate the same DB table.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Change Data Capture (CDC) tailing the database WAL/binlog (via Debezium + Kafka) decouples cache invalidation from application code and guarantees eventual convergence.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: In production distributed systems, cache invalidation manifests across several distinct architectural classifications, operational modes, and implementation strategies:
bullets: **Synchronous App-Level Delete (`DEL` after DB commit)**: Focuses on zero replication lag between db write and cache invalidation on the happy path. Best suited for Single-service ownership where one microservice owns both the DB table and the Redis cache..

**Asynchronous CDC (Debezium WAL -> Kafka -> Invalidator)**: Focuses on guaranteed at-least-once invalidation; decouples writers from cache key topology. Best suited for Large architectures with multiple writers, composite caches, or multi-region replication..

How Leases Work: On a cache miss, the cache grants Reader A a 64-bit lease token. When Writer B calls `DEL key`, the cache invalidates any outstanding lease tokens for that key. When Reader A belatedly calls `SET key v1 (with lease)`, the cache rejects the write because the lease was invalidated!

Database-Generated Monotonic Versions: In Redis, store a hash containing `version` (or DB `xmin`/`updated_at_ns`) and use a Lua script on cache population that only overwrites if the incoming version is strictly greater.

Namespace / Generation Token (Epoch Key): Instead of deleting 500 pagination keys for `merchant:42`, store a version integer at `merchant:42:epoch` (e.g., `7`) and construct list keys as `merchant:42:v7:page:1`. Incrementing `epoch` to `8` instantly invalidates all pages in O(1)!

L1 In-Process Cache Invalidation: Use Redis Client-Side Caching (RESP3 invalidation tracking) or Redis Pub/Sub / Kafka broadcast to notify all application pods to evict keys from their local RAM caches.

codeSnippet.title: Race-Free Cache Population Using Lua Version Check
codeSnippet.code:
-- Lua script: Only populate or update cache if incoming DB version > cached version
-- Prevents slow cache-miss readers from overwriting newer invalidations/tombstones!
local currentVersion = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ver') or '0')
local incomingVersion = tonumber(ARGV[1])

if incomingVersion > currentVersion then
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'ver', ARGV[1], 'data', ARGV[2])
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[3]))
  return 1
end
return 0

-- On Write Invalidation: Instead of raw DEL (which forgets the version),
-- write a short-lived tombstone with the new version and empty data!

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Adopting appropriate design patterns around cache invalidation unlocks critical performance, scalability, and operational advantages for modern backend platforms:
bullets: **Where to Use — High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Single-service ownership where one microservice owns both the DB table and the Redis cache. and environments requiring Zero replication lag between DB write and cache invalidation on the happy path..

**Where to Use — High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Large architectures with multiple writers, composite caches, or multi-region replication. where Guaranteed at-least-once invalidation; decouples writers from cache key topology..

**How to Use — Engineering Implementation**: Invalidating a single entity key (`user:123`) is straightforward, but what about cached list queries (`merchant:42:products:page:1`) or in-memory L1 caches inside 100 Node.js/Java application pods?. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: While essential for scalable engineering, cache invalidation introduces substantial architectural trade-offs, operational failure modes, and anti-patterns if applied inappropriately:
bullets: **Where to Avoid — Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints impose prone to partial failure if app crashes after db commit; tightly couples all writers to cache keys.
**Where to Avoid — Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid premature optimization when introduces 20–100ms pipeline lag between db commit and cache eviction.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Mastering cache invalidation is a defining trait of Staff-level distributed systems engineers. Navigating the delicate balance between performance, reliability, and simplicity ensures architectures scale sustainably without introducing unmanageable operational friction.
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Memcached Leases (or Redis version tokens) solve the classic Stale-Set race condition between a concurrent cache-miss reader and an invalidating writer.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Referencing the 'Namespace Epoch Key' trick for invalidating paginated lists in O(1) and 'Lease Tokens / Tombstone Versions' to prevent stale cache-miss sets demonstrates Staff-level mastery.
